title: Causal memory and structural complexity of a quantum space series
abstract: What makes one quantum process more complex than another? We adopt an operational approach inspired by classical complexity science, which characterises structure through the memory required for causal generation. We develop a fully-quantum extension of computational mechanics for quantum space series: Sequences of quantum outputs that do not return to interact with their generator. For stationary, memoryful quantum space series admitting finite-dimensional, primitive causal models, we show that a memory-minimal model can be chosen to generate the outputs isometrically, without a discarded environment. The resulting canonical matrix product state representation determines both the minimum memory dimension and the minimum memory entropy. The latter is precisely the entanglement entropy across the past-future bipartition, giving entanglement an operational interpretation as irreducible memory for causal generation. Within this class, we further establish a vanishing fundamental entropy rate, the absence of causal asymmetry, and infinite quantum Markov order. These results establish an operational framework for quantifying intrinsic quantum structure, revealing deep connections between causal generation, complexity, memory, entropy, and entanglement.
summary: This paper establishes an operational framework to quantify the complexity of quantum processes by defining it in terms of the minimum memory required for their causal generation. It shows that for a specific class of quantum systems, this minimum memory is quantitatively equal to the entanglement entropy across the past-future cut. This deepens the understanding of entanglement by giving it a concrete role as the irreducible memory resource governing quantum structure.
main_problem: To develop an operational framework to quantify the intrinsic structural complexity of quantum processes by measuring the minimum memory required for their causal generation.
main_result: The quantum statistical complexity of the process is shown to be precisely equal to the entanglement entropy across the past-future bipartition, providing an operational meaning to entanglement as irreducible memory.
method: The authors extend classical complexity science to quantum systems by analyzing quantum space series using a fully-quantum extension of computational mechanics and matrix product state representations.
model_or_system: The focus is on stationary, memoryful quantum space series, modeled as sequences of quantum outputs generated by a memory system undergoing time-invariant unitary evolution.
key_observables: Memory dimension, minimum memory entropy, entanglement entropy (across past-future cut), fundamental entropy rate, and causal asymmetry.
important_parameters: Stationarity, finite-dimensional primitive causal models, and the structure of the memory channel $\Lambda_q$.
main_assumptions: The analysis is restricted to quantum space series that admit finite-dimensional, primitive causal models, and the process is assumed to be stationary.
figures_summary: Figure 1 illustrates a quantum space series as a one-dimensional array of spatially-correlated quantum systems emitted by a memory system, with the evolution represented by a unitary operator.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining the problem (operational complexity via memory) to formalizing the quantum system (quantum space series, unitary evolution) and deriving key mathematical results linking memory bounds, entanglement entropy, and the resulting canonical matrix product state representation.
why_interesting: This work provides a rigorous, information-theoretic measure of complexity for open quantum systems, directly linking fundamental concepts like entanglement and memory in a way that is highly relevant to understanding quantum dynamics and correlations in many-body physics.

figures.caption: FIG. 1. Quantum space series. (a) A quantum space series ←→ ρ consists of a one-dimensional array of spatially-correlated quantum systems, emitted by the time-invariant evolution of a persistent memory system σ. (b) This evolution can be rep- resented by a unitary evolution U acting on the memory and two blank ancillae at each timestep, with one of the resulting ancillae becoming the space series output for that timestep, and the other containing ‘junk’ that is discarded into the en- vironment.

FIG. 2. Examples. (a,b) Growth of quantum block entropy with increasing sequence length for the quantum perturbed coin and quantum Nemo processes at various parameter values, all showing convergence to the excess quantum entropy. (c,d) Analogous plots for the myopic fundamental entropy rate, all showing convergence to hq = 0.
